newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China soybean policy seen increasing import demand.
newsitem.headline: China soybean policy seen increasing import demand.

text.p: China's demand for soybeans and soymeal could soar in 1997 as the principal growing province sticks to its policy of not allowing beans to move outside its borders and the domestic crop falls, traders said on Thursday.
China's seemingly insatiable demand for soymeal, which will see around 1.1 million tonnes of imports in 1996, is underpinning world prices, they said.

With an expected drop in soybean production in November, and protectionist policies in Heilongjiang, the main growing province, China's need for meal and bean imports in the coming year could squeeze world supply, the traders added.

Heilongjiang's moratorium on the sale of soybeans to other provinces, confirmed officially on Wednesday, "means that prices in Heilongjiang will be kept low, and prices in the rest of the country will be kept high," one trader in Hong Kong said.
Chinese authorities favour the policy as it has kept domestic soybean market prices low and state grain bureaux did not therefore need to raise the price paid to farmers for set quotas of soybeans.
"If they abolish this policy, everyone will rush to Heilongjiang to buy beans and the price will go up -- then the government will not be able to procure them," the trader said.
"As it is, the farmers will get discouraged with the low prices, and soybean production will drop year by year. There is only one way to go with this policy, and that's down," he said.

As a result, demand will rise for beans and meal -- a high protein byproduct left over from the crushing of soybeans for oil and used in animal feed -- traders said. The big question is -- by how much.
One particularly bullish Asian trader predicted China's 1997 total soybean and soymeal imports at 2.5 million tonnes.
Others were not so bullish, but said 1997 would be open season for beans, especially as now-high vegetable oil stocks run low and bean crushers strive to keep busy.
China imported up to 600,000 tonnes of soymeal in the first half of 1996, with another 500,000 expected to arrive before year-end, the Chinese Futures Herald newspaper reported.

Domestic soymeal prices have risen by 1,140 yuan (US$137) a tonne since May to reach more than 3,000 yuan (US$361) in August. Last year's production drop and a subsequent increase in demand by a million tonnes were to blame, it said.
"The only thing keeping meal going (on the world market) is China, and the only thing keeping China going is the favourable tax policy (on meal)," a source in Singapore said.
China levies a 13 percent value-added tax (VAT) on top of a three percent import duty on beans. Meal is subject to only a five percent import duty and no VAT.
A change in this tax structure would be a boon for growers and consumers, traders say.

"If they put the duty on the meal and reduced the duty on beans it would balance the picture a little bit," another Asian trader said. "It should be the other way round, so they do tolling (processing) instead of driving prices up.
"The crushers need beans," he said.
Soybean and meal producers in India and the United States could benefit from China's deficit, traders said.
But prices, which would normally ease as new crops became available, would remain high as long as the market perceived high Chinese demand, traders said.
Current Chinese buying interest is steady below $310 a tonne, still around $10 a tonne below prevailing c&f (cost and freight) offers, traders said.
China's soy product imports would begin in earnest towards year-end, traders said, with substantial quantities seen arriving in time for Chinese New Year around February.
Traders predicted a fall in 1996 soybean output of more than a million tonnes to around 11.5-11.8 million tonnes.

China's soybean harvest last November was said by trade and industry sources to be down at least 20 percent on 1994's bumper 16.3 million tonnes. Consumption in calendar year 1995 was 19.5 million tonnes, Chinese press reports said.
